note: Written to be spoken: one sentence or phrase per line; {"beat": s} is a deliberate pause; code is spelled the way it is said. `answer` plays after the learner answers a predict step.

lines: The last reel's vector only grew.
This one gives memory back.
A pop that leaves it less than half full halves its capacity... and copies every key.
Start full, at sixteen keys. Push once. Then repeat: pop, pop, push, push.
One unit of cost is one element write. A pop costs one.
The rules again. A full vector doubles on a push. A pop that leaves it less than half full halves it.
Both copy every key.
From seventeen keys in capacity thirty two, how many element writes does one round of pop, pop, push, push cost?
answer: Thirty five. One, plus sixteen, plus one, plus seventeen.
The second pop leaves fifteen keys in thirty two. That is under half, so it halves to sixteen, and copies fifteen.
Now fifteen of sixteen slots are full, so the second push finds the vector full, and doubles it, copying sixteen.
The round ends where it began. So every round costs the same.

lines: After the fill, every round repeats.
Eight rounds cost two hundred eighty writes. Three hundred twenty eight in all.
Each round copies nearly the whole vector... twice.
Per operation, the rounds cost two C plus three, divided by four. That grows with C.
At C equal to sixteen it is eight point seven five. At about a million, it is more than five hundred twenty four thousand.
No fixed charge can pay for that.
An adversary only has to choose the sequence.
Fill with about half of n pushes first, and n operations cost theta of n squared.
The last reel stored credits on elements.
Now keep the savings as one number, for the whole structure.
Call it phi.
The amortized cost of an operation is its actual cost, plus phi after the operation, minus phi before it.
For the counter, phi is the number of one bits.
Add one to seven. Four bits flip, and phi falls from three to one.
The amortized cost is two, like every increment.
Add up the amortized costs, and every phi in the middle cancels.
Each plus phi meets the minus phi on the next line.
Only the ends survive. The amortized total is the actual total, plus the last phi, minus the first.
Start phi at zero, never let it go negative, and the amortized total bounds the actual total after every operation.
Tarjan calls this the physicist's view. He credits it to Sleator, and calls it entirely equivalent to the banker's credits.
The stack's coins sat on its keys. So phi is the number of keys.
A push costs one, and raises phi by one. Amortized cost, two.
A multipop of k keys costs k, and lowers phi by k. Amortized cost, zero.
Tarjan's opening stack, with some pops and then a push in each operation, gets the same bound: at most twice the number of operations.
Which potential makes every append constant amortized?
It must drop on append nine, which copies eight keys, and rise only a little on the cheap appends.
answer: Phi equals two n minus cap. Twice the keys past the midpoint... Blum's piggy bank.
Each cheap append raises it by two. Just before a resize it equals n, exactly the keys to copy. Just after, it is two.
So append nine costs nine minus six, which is three. So does every append but the first.
The other three potentials don't drop when the copy comes.

lines: Here is that gauge on the vector.
Phi equals two n minus cap says how far the vector is from where a grow leaves it.
Just after a grow, it is two. When the vector is full, it is n... exactly the keys the next grow copies.
The actual costs spike. The amortized costs are flat at three, and two for the first append.
It is the last reel's bank, without its spare coin.
Now let the vector shrink, and keep the same potential.
Pops drive it down. At half full it reaches zero, and then it keeps going, below zero.
After two pops it is minus two, and the amortized total, forty eight, is already less than the actual total, fifty.
A potential that can go negative proves nothing.
Below half full the vector is saving for its shrink, so its potential has to grow again there.
Write alpha for n over cap, the load factor.
Charge for the distance from half full, in either direction.
Phi is two n minus cap when alpha is at least a half. It is cap over two, minus n, when alpha is below a half.
It is never negative, and zero at half full.
At full it is cap, which pays for the next grow's copies. At a quarter full it is cap over four, which pays for the next shrink's.
Under shrink at a quarter, a pop takes the vector from eight keys in capacity thirty two, to seven. That is under a quarter.
It halves to sixteen and copies seven. Actual cost, eight.
With the two piece potential, what is its amortized cost?
answer: One.
Before, alpha is a quarter, and phi is sixteen minus eight, which is eight.
After, seven keys in sixteen, and phi is eight minus seven, which is one.
So the amortized cost is eight, plus one, minus eight. One.
The pops from half full down to a quarter each paid two, one for the pop and one into phi. The shrink spends what they saved.

lines: Every case, checked.
A push costs at most three amortized. A pop, at most two. Including the ones that resize.
So any m pushes and pops from empty cost at most three m.
Amortized constant, for both, for every sequence.
The code checks every reachable state, up to capacity four thousand ninety six.
A resize is paid for only if phi falls by about what it copies.
Under shrink at a quarter, the pops down to a quarter fill the gauge, and the shrink spends it.
Under shrink at a half, the shrink fires at half full, where phi is zero. It lands at fifteen of sixteen, nearly full.
Phi jumps to fourteen, and that pop costs thirty amortized... growing with the vector.
This is resize hysteresis.
The grow and shrink thresholds must leave a gap proportional to the capacity.
So that after any resize, omega of cap operations pass before the next one... enough to refill the gauge.
Halving at a quarter lands the vector near half full. Halving at a half lands it one push from full.
Any fixed shrink fraction below a half works.
The same move proves bounds you will meet later.
Splay trees: phi is the sum of log base two of every subtree's size. That is Sleator and Tarjan.
Fibonacci heaps: the trees in the root list, plus twice the marked nodes.
Union find: Tarjan analysed it in nineteen seventy five, and potential proofs now reach its bound, order alpha of n, where alpha of n is the inverse Ackermann function.
Back to the problem.
Under shrink at a quarter, the same forty nine operations cost eighty writes, not three hundred twenty eight.
After the one grow, nothing resizes. And the potential proves at most three per push and two per pop, for every sequence.
But the push that copied sixteen keys is still a single operation.
A request waiting on it still waits.
A teammate reuses phi equals two n minus cap, for a vector that grows by one and a half.
Append thirteen finds twelve keys in capacity twelve, grows to eighteen, and copies twelve. Actual cost, thirteen.
What is its amortized cost under that phi?
answer: Nine.
Before, phi is twenty four minus twelve, which is twelve. After, twenty six minus eighteen, which is eight.
The gauge drops only four, because growing by one and a half leaves the vector two thirds full, not half.
So the amortized cost is thirteen minus four. Nine. And it keeps growing with the vector.
Use three n minus two cap instead, zero at two thirds. Then every append costs at most four.

lines: Fill the vector to two to the twentieth keys, more than a million. Push once.
Then run one thousand rounds of pop, pop, push, push, under shrink at a half.
About how many element writes do the thousand rounds cost?
answer: About two point one billion.
One thousand times two C plus three: two billion, ninety seven million, one hundred fifty five thousand writes. Almost all of them copies.
Under shrink at a quarter: four thousand. One per operation.
With C fixed, the thrash costs order C per operation. Theta of n squared for n operations needs C to grow with n.

lines: Start full at sixteen keys, and strictly alternate push, pop.
Rule A halves when a pop leaves the vector less than half full. Rule B, when it leaves it at most half full.
Which rules thrash?
answer: Only B.
After the first push there are seventeen keys in thirty two. A pop leaves sixteen... exactly half.
Rule A does not shrink, and the next push fits. Alternation costs one per operation after the grow.
Rule B shrinks to sixteen, which is full, and the next push doubles again. Seventeen writes, every operation.
Rule A still thrashes on pop, pop, push, push. The gap must be a fraction of the capacity, not one key.
